title: Die Kornähre
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 2, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 194. Text from Wikisource („Die Kornähre (1857)“, twice proofread against the original). Fresh translation made directly from the German; 1857 spelling preserved exactly.
about: KHM 194 is an aetiological legend, over in a page: in the age when God still walked on the earth a stalk of grain bore kernels its whole length, four and five hundredfold, until a woman tore off a handful of ears to wipe the mud from her child’s dress. The answer is to take the ear away altogether; what stands at the top of the stalk today is the remnant granted back when the bystanders knelt and pleaded — not for themselves, they said, but for the hens, who would otherwise starve. The whole tale exists to explain a thing anyone can still go out and look at.

sentences.t: Vorzeiten, als Gott noch selbst auf Erden wandelte, da war die Fruchtbarkeit des Bodens viel größer als sie jetzt ist:
sentences.l: In former times, when God still walked on earth himself, then the fruitfulness of the soil was much greater than it is now:
sentences.i: In the old days, when God still walked the earth in person, the ground was far more fruitful than it is now:
sentences.n: “auf Erden” keeps an old dative ending that survives only in this fixed phrase — on earth. wandeln here is the elevated verb for walking or going about, not the more common sense of changing. The “da” after the long opening clause is resumptive — it picks the sentence up again and need not be translated. The colon does the work an English semicolon or dash would.

sentences.t: damals trugen die Ähren nicht funfzig- oder sechzigfältig, sondern vier- bis fünfhundertfältig.
sentences.l: at that time the ears of grain bore not fifty- or sixtyfold, but four- to five-hundredfold.
sentences.i: in those days the ears of grain bore not fifty or sixtyfold, but four to five hundredfold.
sentences.n: “funfzig” is the 1857 spelling of fünfzig. The suffix ‑fältig means ‑fold, so many times over; the hyphen after funfzig- holds the place of the shared ‑fältig, exactly as English writes “fifty- or sixtyfold”. die Ähre is the ear of grain — the head at the top of the stalk — and has nothing to do with die Ehre, honour.

sentences.t: Da wuchsen die Körner am Halm von unten bis oben hinauf: so lang er war, so lang war auch die Ähre.
sentences.l: Then the grains grew on the stalk from below right up to the top: as long as it was, so long was the ear too.
sentences.i: The grains grew on the stalk from the bottom all the way up: however long the stalk was, just so long was the ear.
sentences.n: “so lang er war, so lang war auch” is the German correlative pattern — as … so … — with the verb in second place in both halves. The er is der Halm, the stalk.

sentences.t: Aber wie die Menschen sind, im Überfluß achten sie des Segens nicht mehr, der von Gott kommt, werden gleichgültig und leichtsinnig.
sentences.l: But as people are, in abundance they heed the blessing no more, which comes from God, become indifferent and thoughtless.
sentences.i: But such is the way of people: in plenty they no longer take heed of the blessing that comes from God, and grow indifferent and careless.
sentences.n: achten takes the genitive here — “achten sie des Segens nicht” — an older construction where modern German would say achten auf den Segen. The relative clause “der von Gott kommt” has been pushed past its noun to the end of the sentence, which German allows freely and English does not.

sentences.t: Eines Tages gieng eine Frau an einem Kornfeld vorbei,
sentences.l: One day a woman went past a cornfield,
sentences.i: One day a woman was walking past a field of grain,
sentences.n: “eines Tages” is a genitive of time — of a day, meaning one day; German uses the genitive this way for indefinite points in time. vorbeigehen is separable: gieng … vorbei. “gieng” is the 1857 spelling of ging.

sentences.t: und ihr kleines Kind, das neben ihr sprang, fiel in eine Pfütze und beschmutzte sein Kleidchen.
sentences.l: and her little child, that was skipping beside her, fell into a puddle and dirtied its little dress.
sentences.i: and her little child, skipping along at her side, fell into a puddle and dirtied its little dress.
sentences.n: das Kind is neuter, so German says “sein Kleidchen” — literally “its little dress” — with no comment on whether the child is a boy or a girl. The two diminutives, Kleidchen and the earlier kleines, keep the scale of the thing small and domestic.

sentences.t: Da riß die Mutter eine Hand voll der schönen Ähren ab und reinigte ihm damit das Kleid.
sentences.l: Then the mother tore off a handful of the beautiful ears and cleaned the dress for it with them.
sentences.i: Then the mother tore off a handful of the fine ears of grain and wiped the child’s dress clean with them.
sentences.n: abreißen is separable: riß … ab. “eine Hand voll” is written as two words in 1857 where modern German has the single noun eine Handvoll. “reinigte ihm … das Kleid” uses the dative of the person — cleaned the dress for it — where English prefers a possessive.

sentences.t: Als der Herr, der eben vorüberkam, das sah, zürnte er und sprach „fortan soll der Kornhalm keine Ähre mehr tragen: die Menschen sind der himmlischen Gabe nicht länger werth.“
sentences.l: When the Lord, who was just coming past, saw that, he grew angry and said “from now on the corn-stalk shall bear no ear any more: people are no longer worthy of the heavenly gift.”
sentences.i: When the Lord, who happened to be passing, saw it, he was angry and said “from this time on the stalk of grain shall bear no ear at all: people are no longer worthy of the gift of heaven.”
sentences.n: “eben” here is temporal — just then, at that very moment. “der himmlischen Gabe … werth” takes the genitive: worthy of. “werth” is the 1857 spelling of wert. The tale states its theology flatly and without softening: the loss is a punishment.

sentences.t: Die Umstehenden, die das hörten, erschraken, fielen auf die Knie und flehten, daß er noch etwas möchte an dem Halm stehen lassen:
sentences.l: Those standing round, who heard that, took fright, fell on their knees and pleaded that he might still let something remain on the stalk:
sentences.i: The bystanders who heard it took fright, fell on their knees and begged that he would let something still remain on the stalk:
sentences.n: die Umstehenden is an adjective used as a noun — “the standing-around ones”, the bystanders. “möchte” is subjunctive inside the reported plea, and “stehen lassen” is two words in 1857 for what modern German writes as one, stehenlassen — to let stand.

sentences.t: wenn sie selbst es auch nicht verdienten, doch der unschuldigen Hühner wegen, die sonst verhungern müßten.
sentences.l: even if they themselves did not deserve it, yet for the sake of the innocent hens, which would otherwise have to starve.
sentences.i: [saying that] even if they themselves did not deserve it, it should still be for the sake of the innocent hens, which would otherwise have to starve.
sentences.n: The plea runs on without a verb of its own — German lets the reported speech continue where English needs a fresh start, so the idiomatic line supplies “[saying that]” in square brackets. “wegen” follows its noun here, “der unschuldigen Hühner wegen”, which is the older word order; modern German more often puts it in front. “verdienten” and “müßten” are both subjunctive, keeping the whole clause inside the reported plea.

sentences.t: Der Herr, der ihr Elend voraus sah, erbarmte sich und gewährte die Bitte.
sentences.l: The Lord, who foresaw their misery, took pity and granted the request.
sentences.i: The Lord, who saw their distress coming, was moved to pity and granted the request.
sentences.n: “voraus sah” is the separable voraussehen — to see in advance — printed as two words, as 1857 German often prints such verbs. sich erbarmen is reflexive: to be moved to pity. die Bitte is the noun — the request — from bitten, to ask.

sentences.t: Also blieb noch oben die Ähre übrig, wie sie jetzt wächst.
sentences.l: Thus there was still the ear left over at the top, as it grows now.
sentences.i: And so the ear was left at the top, just as it grows today.
sentences.n: “also” in 1857 German means thus, and so — not the modern English “also”. This is an aetiology: the tale exists to account for why a stalk of grain carries its ear only at the very top.

glossary.achten: achten — to heed, to pay heed to (here with the genitive: des Segens achten, to heed the blessing)
glossary.bitte: die Bitte — request, plea (noun; from bitten, to ask)
glossary.erbarmte: sich erbarmen — took pity, was moved to pity (3rd sg. past, reflexive: erbarmte sich)
glossary.herr: der Herr — the Lord (here God himself, walking on earth); also lord, master
glossary.ihm: ihm — to it, for it (dative; here of das Kind, which is neuter, so English says ‘its’)
glossary.lassen: lassen — to let, to allow (here stehen lassen: to let stand, to leave standing)
glossary.tragen: tragen — to bear, to carry (of a stalk: to bear an ear of grain)
glossary.trugen: tragen — bore, yielded (3rd pl. past; of grain, to bear so many fold)
glossary.verdienten: verdienen — deserved, merited (3rd pl. past subjunctive here: wenn sie es nicht verdienten)
glossary.wandelte: wandeln — to walk, go about (3rd sg. past; elevated: auf Erden wandeln, to walk the earth)
